"Northern Territory police failed to act on a string of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles before the death of a vulnerable 23-year-old man last year, a coroner has found. NT coroner Greg Cavanagh has criticised police for failing to act on an internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged vehicles in 2013, following an earlier death in custody. In the three years between the two deaths, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in caged vehicles. "In six cases the persons were not detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious," Cavanagh found. "It wasn't a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when."

On 16 September last year, two officers were making their way through Darwin, on their way to investigate a noise complaint, when they came across the scene of a serious crash. A Toyota Hilux had smashed into a palm tree on the corner of the Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, not far from Darwin airport. Hiding behind some vegetation was Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23. Walkinshaw was unharmed but held his passenger in his arms. The young woman, whom he had met earlier at a bar, was in and out of consciousness, having suffered an injury to her back. Walkinshaw was well over the limit, returning a reading of 0.149.

The officers called for medical assistance for the injured woman and placed Walkinshaw under arrest for drink driving and dangerous driving offences. Visibly distraught over what had happened to his passenger, Walkinshaw was placed in the caged section of the police vehicle — a confined metal compartment in the rear of the van separated from the cabin by a solid partition. The officers could neither see nor hear the young man once the door was shut.

During the drive to the watch house, the officers did not check on Walkinshaw. There was no CCTV camera installed in the cage, despite the 2013 internal recommendation that such cameras be fitted as a matter of urgency. When they arrived at the custody facility approximately 20 minutes later, officers opened the rear door to find Walkinshaw unresponsive. He had used his shirt to fashion a ligature, attaching it to a fixture inside the cage. Paramedics were called but were unable to revive him. He was pronounced dead shortly after.

The coronial inquest revealed a deeply troubling pattern of institutional neglect. Coroner Cavanagh heard evidence that Walkinshaw had been in a highly emotional state at the time of his arrest, expressing extreme guilt and distress about the injuries sustained by his passenger. Despite exhibiting clear signs of vulnerability, no mental health assessment was conducted before he was placed in the vehicle, and no welfare checks were carried out during the journey.

The inquest further uncovered that the 2013 report, commissioned after a separate death in custody involving similar circumstances, had made several key recommendations. Chief among them was the installation of CCTV cameras in all caged police vehicles, improved protocols for assessing the mental state of detainees before transport, and mandatory periodic checks during transit. None of these recommendations had been implemented by the time of Walkinshaw's death.

Evidence presented to the coroner showed that in the intervening three years, at least 16 people had attempted suicide or serious self-harm in caged police vehicles across the Northern Territory. In some cases, individuals had used clothing, shoelaces, or other items to attempt to hang themselves from fixtures inside the cages. Several had been found unconscious or barely breathing when officers finally opened the doors.

"The failure to implement these recommendations is inexcusable," Cavanagh wrote in his findings. "Police command was aware of the risks. They had been told in clear terms what needed to be done. The cost of installing cameras was modest. The cost of inaction has been measured in human lives."

Walkinshaw's family told the inquest that Dale had no history of mental illness or suicidal ideation. His mother described him as a young man who loved the outdoors and had recently started a new job in construction. She said the family was devastated not only by his death but by the knowledge that it could have been prevented.

"My son made a terrible mistake that night," she said in a statement read to the court. "He should have faced the consequences of that mistake. He should have had the chance to make amends. Instead, he was locked in a metal box where no one could see him or hear him, and he died alone."

The coroner made several recommendations, including the immediate installation of CCTV cameras in all caged police vehicles, the development of mandatory risk assessment protocols for all persons taken into police custody, and the implementation of a policy requiring officers to conduct visual welfare checks on detainees at regular intervals during transport. He also recommended that the Northern Territory government consider redesigning the caged vehicle compartments to remove potential ligature points.

NT Police Commissioner Reece Kershaw issued a statement following the release of the findings, expressing condolences to the Walkinshaw family and acknowledging the failures identified by the coroner. He said the force had already begun a program to install cameras in its fleet of caged vehicles and was reviewing its custody transport procedures.

Aboriginal legal services and civil liberties groups called the findings damning, noting that Indigenous Australians are disproportionately represented among those transported in caged police vehicles and among deaths in custody nationally. They called for broader reforms to policing practices in the Northern Territory and renewed their calls for full implementation of the recommendations from the 1991 Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody.

The young woman who was injured in the crash survived her injuries but was left with lasting spinal damage. She told reporters outside the court that she felt profound sadness for Walkinshaw's family. "He stayed with me after the crash," she said. "He held me and told me help was coming. He was scared, but he didn't leave me. That's the person he was."

Coroner Cavanagh concluded his findings with a pointed observation: "When authorities are warned of a foreseeable risk to life and fail to act, and when that failure leads to death, there must be accountability. Dale Walkinshaw's death was preventable. The systems that should have protected him failed at every level.""
